items.question: An acceptance evaluation set is agreed at the end of discovery and will decide whether the system is signed off. Which TWO properties must it have for that decision to be defensible? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: It contains only cases the current human process handles correctly, so the comparison is fair to the system.
options.B: It is frozen and withheld before prompt development begins, so no case in it shaped how the system was built.
options.C: It is generated by the model itself from the requirements, to maximise coverage of edge cases nobody thought of.
options.D: It contains an equal number of cases in every category, regardless of how often each one occurs in production.
options.E: Its case mix reflects the production distribution, including the exception classes discovery identified.

items.question: A hospital trust asks for Claude to 'reduce the time clinicians spend on discharge summaries'. Which THREE discovery findings would indicate that the request is primarily a process or data problem rather than a language model problem? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Time-and-motion sampling shows most elapsed time is spent waiting for pharmacy to confirm the medication list, not composing text.
options.B: Consultants dictate summaries in free text, and phrasing, ordering and section headings vary widely between individual consultants and specialties.
options.C: The summary's content sits in three systems, one reachable only through a nightly export that lands after most discharges have happened.
options.D: The record system already auto-populates the summary, and the real complaint is re-keying the same content into a separate GP portal.
options.E: Junior doctors report the hardest part is judging which findings from a long admission are clinically relevant to the receiving GP.

items.question: A council has two hours for a discovery workshop on automating disabled-parking-badge application assessment. Invited so far: the service manager, two team leaders, the IT business partner and a supplier account manager. Which addition would most improve what the session produces?

options.A: Two assessors who process applications daily, with ten recent applications including two refusals.
options.B: The council's chief executive, to signal senior commitment and unblock the programme's funding at cabinet.
options.C: The supplier's solution architect, to set out the integration and licensing options available for the platform.
options.D: A member of the communications team, to begin planning the public announcement to existing badge holders.

items.question: An insurer's discovery for a claims-note summariser surfaces a conflict between the two units co-funding it. Claims operations want summaries under 100 words so handlers can read them at pace across a high caseload. The fraud team wants every inconsistency between the claimant's statements preserved, which on contested claims runs past 400 words. Contested claims are about 6% of volume. How should discovery resolve this?

options.A: Set a single 250-word cap on every summary as a compromise both the claims and the fraud team can sign up to.
options.B: Specify two outputs from one analysis pass: a short handler summary and a separate flagged-inconsistency record for fraud.
options.C: Escalate to the joint sponsor to rule on which unit's requirement takes precedence in the summary specification.
options.D: Adopt the fraud requirement throughout, since the regulatory exposure from a missed inconsistency outweighs handler reading time.

items.question: A business energy supplier is qualifying two candidate actions for an assistant that acts on customer requests end to end. One is emailing a duplicate copy of an invoice. The other is initiating a supplier switch, which under market rules opens a regulated objection window and, once it completes unopposed, can only be undone by a fresh switch taking several weeks. Both actions have similar request volume, and the intent-classification task for each is of comparable difficulty. What should qualification decide?

options.A: Both qualify equally for autonomous execution, since request volume and intent-classification difficulty are the same for each action.
options.B: Neither qualifies for autonomous execution until intent classification is demonstrated above 99% on a held-out set of real requests.
options.C: Invoice reissue can execute autonomously; switch initiation needs explicit customer confirmation and a staff-reversible hold before submission.
options.D: Both qualify provided every action is written to an immutable log alongside the transcript that triggered it, giving a full audit trail for disputes.

items.question: In week eight of a nine-week discovery at a freight forwarder, with the design nearly signed off, a customs subject matter expert mentions that any automated customs declaration must be lodged through the national customs gateway, which accepts a specific XML schema and authenticates with a per-individual digital certificate held by each operations clerk. No service credential exists in the scheme as far as anyone present knows. The value case assumed end-to-end automated lodgement. What is the best next step?

options.A: Record certificate and schema handling as an implementation detail in the build backlog, and sign the design off on the agreed week-nine date.
options.B: Redesign around a shared service account and open a formal request with the national customs authority to have one issued before the build starts.
options.C: Permanently remove customs lodgement from scope and deliver only the internal booking and documentation parts of the workflow.
options.D: Re-open feasibility on lodgement alone: check whether a non-individual credential exists, and if not, make the clerk the lodging actor and re-cost.

items.question: Which TWO characteristics most reliably indicate that a task belongs to a language model rather than to deterministic rules or a classical statistical model? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The task produces a numeric value that must be reproducible to the penny whenever an auditor asks.
options.B: The task runs at very high volume on inputs arriving in a fixed schema that has not changed in years.
options.C: Inputs arrive as natural language or documents and vary in ways nobody can enumerate in advance.
options.D: The organisation already holds a large, cleanly labelled training set covering the task's categories.
options.E: The output requires judgement that written policy describes but no decision table can capture.

items.question: Why should a discovery business case compare the proposed Claude system against the best available non-AI improvement to the same process, rather than only against the current state?

options.A: Measuring only against today's process credits the model with gains a cheaper process or integration fix would also deliver.
options.B: Financial regulators require a documented alternatives analysis to be filed with the supervisor before any AI system may be deployed.
options.C: It is the only reliable way to derive the latency and throughput budget the new system will have to meet in production.
options.D: Non-AI alternatives are almost always cheaper, so the comparison usually ends the project early and saves discovery time.

items.question: A specialty chemicals manufacturer runs one Claude system in production: question answering over a curated safety-data-sheet corpus, with a retrieval pipeline, an evaluation harness and a review workflow the regulatory function has accepted. Discovery has capacity for exactly one more build, and the programme must show value within one quarter to secure continuing funding. Candidates are: summarising customer complaint emails (new corpus, new consumers, highest volume); answering regulatory compliance questions over the same curated corpus for a different internal team; an autonomous agent that raises purchase orders; and a demand-forecasting capability. Which should be selected?

options.A: Complaint email summarisation, because it carries the highest volume of the four candidates and therefore the largest measurable time saving in the quarter.
options.B: Regulatory compliance questions over the same curated corpus, because the retrieval pipeline, evaluation harness and accepted review workflow all carry over.
options.C: The purchase order agent, because demonstrating autonomous action end to end makes the strongest case to the continuing-funding committee.
options.D: Demand forecasting, because broadening from language into predictive work widens the programme's remit and its future funding base.

items.question: A building society is scoping an assistant to handle mortgage arrears enquiries. Its vulnerable-customer policy instructs advisers to 'escalate where vulnerability is suspected' and gives illness, bereavement and job loss as examples. The architect must specify when the assistant hands off to a human. What is the most useful elicitation move?

options.A: Ask the compliance function to write an operational definition of vulnerability, with worked tests, that the assistant can apply directly to each call.
options.B: Configure the assistant to hand off whenever illness, bereavement or job loss is mentioned, mirroring the three examples the policy itself gives.
options.C: Have the assistant hand off whenever its own reported confidence in the arrears response falls below an agreed numeric threshold.
options.D: Review the last hundred escalations advisers raised with the recorded trigger, alongside comparable calls not escalated, and derive the boundary.

items.question: A field service operation asks for Claude to build each day's engineer schedule, minimising travel while respecting engineer skills, parts availability and customer appointment windows. Why does this fail qualification as a language model task?

options.A: Schedules change through the day as jobs overrun and parts fail to arrive, so a model cannot be re-run often enough.
options.B: The model cannot emit output in the calendar format the dispatch system and the engineers' mobile app require.
options.C: It is a constrained optimisation; a solver returns a provably feasible assignment, or proves that none exists.
options.D: Scheduling needs live van stock and engineer location data that cannot be supplied to a model at request time.

items.question: A hotel group asks for Claude to deduplicate 14 million guest profiles held across four property systems, merging records that refer to the same person. The fields available are name, email, phone, address, loyalty number and date of birth, and roughly 2% of records are believed to be duplicates. What should discovery conclude?

options.A: Deterministic keys plus blocking and probabilistic linkage resolve most of it cheaply; reserve the model for the residual ambiguous pairs.
options.B: Use the model for every pairwise comparison, since it handles name variants, transliteration and address abbreviation better than string metrics.
options.C: Process all 14 million profiles in a small number of very large context windows so the model can see the whole population at once and cluster it.
options.D: Decline the request; deduplicating the guest master is a data governance activity for the chief data officer, outside the AI programme's remit.

items.question: A medical device manufacturer is defining acceptance for a Claude system that drafts sections of technical files submitted to notified bodies. The proposed criterion is that 95% of generated sections are judged acceptable by a reviewer. Discovery establishes that a named regulatory affairs specialist reviews and signs every section before submission, and that one error class — citing the wrong version of a harmonised standard — previously caused a submission rejection and a six-week delay. The standards register is an internal system with an exact list of current versions. What should be added to the criteria?

options.A: Raise the aggregate threshold from 95% to 99% so that the residual error rate is small enough for a notified-body submission.
options.B: Replace reviewer judgement with a model-graded rubric over the drafted sections, so the acceptability measure is not subjective.
options.C: Measure acceptability separately per specialist and require agreement between two reviewers before a section is scored as acceptable.
options.D: Keep the aggregate threshold and add a zero-tolerance criterion for standard-version errors, checked against the standards register.

items.question: Why do mature acceptance criteria state an aggregate quality threshold and, separately, a named set of failure modes each with its own gate?

options.A: Aggregate thresholds are unreliable because evaluation sets are always too small to support them statistically at the required confidence.
options.B: An aggregate averages over failures of very different cost, so a system can clear the threshold and still commit the costly errors.
options.C: Naming failure modes in a documented hazard log is required by most regulators before an automated system may be deployed.
options.D: Named failure modes are easier to remediate than diffuse aggregate quality problems, so listing them shortens the fix cycle.

items.question: What should exist at the close of discovery for design work to begin on a sound footing?

options.A: A signed statement of work, a resourced delivery team and an agreed sprint plan for the first three build sprints.
options.B: A working prototype demonstrated to the executive sponsor and received positively by the programme steering group.
options.C: A problem statement, a measured baseline, acceptance criteria with a frozen set, a named owner and data access.
options.D: A selected model tier, a versioned prompt library and an agreed integration diagram for the target application estate.

items.question: A utility's new-connections team processes supply applications. Nobody has ever measured how long a case takes. The case system records only a created and a closed timestamp, and cases routinely sit dormant for weeks waiting for customer documents, which inflates elapsed time. Discovery has ten working days. Which TWO approaches will produce a usable baseline of actual working time? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Have eight case handlers record start and stop times on a tally sheet for every case they touch across one week.
options.B: Take the median of closed-minus-created elapsed days across every case completed in the last twelve months in the case system.
options.C: Observe three handlers for two days each, timing cases directly and recording waiting time separately from working time.
options.D: Ask the team leader for an estimate of average handling time broken down by case type, and use it as the baseline.
options.E: Divide the team's annual fully-loaded payroll cost by the number of cases the team closed in the same period.

items.question: A national retailer's published policy states no refund without a receipt. Discovery samples 500 refunds across twelve stores: 41% were issued without a receipt where the item could be traced to a loyalty account, applied consistently in every store sampled, and the retailer's own customer satisfaction reporting cites this flexibility as a strength. The assistant being scoped will decide refund eligibility directly. What is the best next step?

options.A: Write the observed rule up as de facto policy with the sampling evidence, and take it to the policy owner for a decision to codify it or stop it.
options.B: Encode the written policy as it stands, since automating an unwritten exception exposes the retailer to inconsistency and discrimination claims.
options.C: Encode the observed loyalty-account practice, since it is the real operating rule and already matches what customers experience in every store.
options.D: Have the assistant decline and hand off to a store colleague whenever no receipt is present, preserving the discretion staff exercise today.

items.question: A European insurer is scoping a policy-question assistant. The business asks for all eleven market languages. Discovery finds three languages account for 84% of contact volume and the remaining eight for 16%; internal staff capable of grading output exist for five languages; and one of the three highest-volume languages has no internal reviewer at all. What scoping decision should discovery recommend?

options.A: Launch all eleven languages, since the model handles them, and add per-language evaluation once traffic accumulates in each market.
options.B: Scope phase one to languages with both meaningful volume and an internal reviewer, gating each later addition on a reviewer.
options.C: Scope by volume alone and launch the three languages that cover 84% of contacts, adding the remaining eight later.
options.D: Launch in English only and let customers switch to their own preferred language themselves in the chat window.

items.question: A stakeholder map plots each party by their influence over the outcome and their interest in it. What is the map primarily for?

options.A: Determining the distribution list for the weekly project status report and the monthly steering pack.
options.B: Establishing the formal approval chain to be followed at the go-live decision point and at each stage gate.
options.C: Selecting which stakeholders should be invited to the discovery workshops and the requirement sessions.
options.D: Setting a differentiated engagement plan and, above all, surfacing high-influence, low-interest parties early.

items.question: A construction group wants Claude to answer 'why did this project's margin move this month?' across 200 live projects. Discovery finds the ERP holds cost and revenue by cost code, but the reason for a variance is discussed in weekly site meetings and recorded, if at all, in a free-text comment field populated on 11% of cost lines, mostly with entries such as 'see email'. The architect sampled 30 of those references and could locate the corresponding email thread for four of them. What should discovery conclude?

options.A: Feasible as asked; the model can infer the cause of each margin movement from the pattern of cost-code movements in the ERP itself, month on month.
options.B: Feasible once the group's email archive is indexed and retrieved alongside the ERP cost lines at answer time, resolving the 'see email' pointers.
options.C: The explanation is recorded nowhere, so the first deliverable is a capture mechanism: a reason code and note taken when the variance is discussed.
options.D: Reject the use case; causal explanation of financial variance across 200 live projects is beyond what a language model can be asked to do.

items.question: A shared services centre's finance director states the success criterion for a Claude invoice-query assistant as 'remove eight full-time roles from the accounts payable team by year end'. The team has 34 people, and the same people perform the second-line check that would catch the assistant's errors. Annual attrition on the team is about 12%. How should the architect handle this in discovery?

options.A: Restate acceptance in terms the system controls — automation rate and cost per resolved query — and flag that cutting the team removes review capacity.
options.B: Decline to accept headcount as a success criterion at all, on the grounds that AI programmes should never be justified by role reduction of any kind.
options.C: Accept the criterion as stated, since eight roles out of thirty-four is unambiguous, measurable and auditable from the payroll system.
options.D: Propose delivering the reduction through the team's natural attrition rather than redundancy, leaving the criterion otherwise unchanged.

items.question: During requirement elicitation, why is it important to collect examples of outputs the business would consider unacceptable, not only examples it considers good?

options.A: Unacceptable examples are required as negative training pairs for any subsequent fine-tuning or preference-tuning work.
options.B: Good examples sit inside the acceptable region; only rejected ones show where its edge is, which guardrails must encode.
options.C: Rejected examples are the documented failure evidence a model risk committee requires before it will approve a system.
options.D: Collecting both kinds roughly halves the number of worked examples needed before the task can be considered specified.

items.question: A prototype that summarises objections to planning applications is rejected by council planning officers on roughly a third of cases. Which THREE findings indicate that the problem is under-specified requirements rather than model capability? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: The summary omits objections that arrived only as scanned handwritten letters attached to the application file in the case system.
options.B: Officers disagree with one another about which objections are material in about 30% of the cases reviewed.
options.C: There is no written rule on whether objections raising non-material planning considerations should be included or excluded.
options.D: The summary occasionally attributes an objection to the wrong address when two neighbouring objectors share a surname and street.
options.E: Officers expect each summary to state the number of distinct objectors, which was never captured as a requirement.

items.question: In week five of an eight-week discovery, a ticketing company's commercial director asks that the web-chat refund assistant also be offered over WhatsApp, 'since it is the same assistant'. Discovery has already established that web chat is authenticated — the customer is signed in and the relevant booking is known — whereas a WhatsApp contact arrives with a phone number only, and 22% of bookings are made by someone other than the traveller. How should the architect respond?

options.A: Add the channel; the delivery surface is a presentation concern and the assistant's refund eligibility logic is entirely unchanged.
options.B: Add the channel, but have the assistant ask the WhatsApp contact to state their booking reference, which it then looks up in the reservation system.
options.C: Decline the request as scope creep arriving too late in the eight-week discovery timetable for the team to absorb it.
options.D: Show the channel breaks the identity assumption the design rests on, so it needs a verification requirement and its own costing.

items.question: Nine weeks into discovery at a logistics software provider, the architect learns in conversation that the firm runs a security architecture review board which meets monthly, and that any product change moving customer data outside the existing service boundary must pass it. The next two meeting agendas are full. Design sign-off is planned in three weeks, the sponsor has never mentioned the board, and the assistant's value depends on answering from each customer's own shipment records. What is the best next step?

options.A: Proceed to design sign-off in three weeks and submit to the board afterwards, since the board reviews product changes rather than architecture designs.
options.B: Ask the sponsor to press the board's chair into convening an extraordinary session for this design ahead of the sign-off date.
options.C: Book the earliest board slot now and reshape remaining discovery to produce what the board assesses — data flows, retention and the boundary change.
options.D: Re-scope the assistant so it never moves customer data outside the existing service boundary, taking the board out of the critical path.

items.question: A gas network operator wants Claude to review contractor method statements against its safety standards before work is authorised. The benefit is avoiding a class of safety incident that occurs about three times a year across roughly 9,000 authorisations. The sponsor asks the architect to propose the success criterion. What should it be?

options.A: Detection rate on a curated set of method statements with known deficiencies, plus the false-flag rate on compliant ones.
options.B: A measured year-on-year reduction in incidents of that class across the network over the first year of operation.
options.C: The number and proportion of method statements the system reviews, since coverage is the benefit the operator directly obtains.
options.D: Reviewer minutes saved per method statement, because safety benefit at this event frequency cannot be measured at all.

items.question: Discovery closes with agreement on who signs the eventual acceptance decision. Which TWO things must that sign-off be recorded against for it to remain meaningful afterwards? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: The specific version of the evaluation set, and the grading method used to produce the score.
options.B: The provider's published capability documentation and benchmark card for the model family in use.
options.C: The number of prompt iterations and evaluation runs the team needed to reach the accepted score.
options.D: The prompt, retrieval configuration and model version the score was obtained with, so it stays identifiable.
options.E: The sponsor's verbal confirmation at the steering committee, captured in the minutes and circulated to attendees.

items.question: An agricultural cooperative wants Claude to extract nitrogen application rates from supplier product labels into an advisory tool used by 4,000 member farms. The product owner proposes 95% extraction accuracy as the requirement. Discovery establishes that an overstated rate leads the farm into a regulatory breach carrying a fine, while an understated rate slightly reduces yield and is usually noticed by the farmer. How should the accuracy requirement be set?

options.A: At 95% overall accuracy as proposed, which is the defensible default for document extraction tasks of this kind across the industry.
options.B: Asymmetrically: a high bar on overstatement, a looser tolerance on understatement, and a refusal path where the label cannot be read.
options.C: At whatever accuracy measurement shows the current manual reading of labels achieves, so the tool is demonstrably no worse than today.
options.D: At 95% with an agronomist reviewing every extraction, which removes the need to distinguish between the two error directions.

items.question: A team establishes a handling-time baseline by sitting with case handlers and timing their work. What is the main threat to that measurement, and the standard mitigation?

options.A: Sample size is too small; mitigate by extending the timing exercise across a full quarter of production casework.
options.B: People work differently when watched, usually faster and more by the book; mitigate by triangulating against system measures.
options.C: Observers' clocks drift apart; mitigate by issuing one shared stopwatch application to everyone taking measurements on the floor.
options.D: Handlers may refuse to take part; mitigate by making participation in the timing study mandatory across the whole team.

items.question: A nuclear decommissioning contractor asks for Claude to draft radiological protection assessments. There are about thirty a year; each takes a qualified specialist roughly three weeks; there are four such specialists and one retires within twelve months. Every assessment is independently checked by a second specialist and approved by the site regulator's inspector. What should qualification conclude?

options.A: Decline: thirty assessments a year cannot justify the build cost, and no evaluation set of usable size can be assembled from that volume.
options.B: Accept with specialist weeks saved per assessment as the success criterion, since three weeks per item is a very large per-unit gain.
options.C: Accept, targeting fully automated drafting of the whole assessment so the capacity lost when the fourth specialist retires is directly replaced.
options.D: Accept, framing the value as retained capacity and captured expertise, with acceptance by expert review against historical assessments.

items.question: A rail operator's AI board holds four qualified use cases with roughly equal estimated annual benefit and equal stakeholder backing. Their data positions differ: the first uses an already-governed, documented, API-accessible incident database; the second needs a data set whose owner has agreed access in principle but which contains personal data requiring an assessment that has not started; the third needs data held only in a supplier's system under a contract silent on the operator's right to use it for automated processing; the fourth needs data that exists but has no owner and no documented schema. Capacity allows two this year and at least one must ship. Which pair, and on what principle?

options.A: The first and the second: sequence on whether a blocker has a named owner and a determinable completion date, not on how large the blocker appears.
options.B: The first and the fourth, on the grounds that an undocumented internal data set is the cheapest blocker to clear because no external party is involved.
options.C: The third and the first, because the supplier contract can be reopened at the next annual review and the pairing spreads risk across dependencies.
options.D: The second and the third, because both blockers are legal in nature and can be cleared by a single legal workstream running alongside the builds.

items.question: Which TWO questions establish a use case's tolerance for error during discovery? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: What accuracy do comparable systems at other firms in this industry publicly report achieving?
options.B: What happens downstream when the output is wrong, and who or what detects the error?
options.C: Which model tier and context window size does the team intend to use for this task?
options.D: How quickly, and at what cost, can a wrong output be reversed once someone has acted on it?
options.E: How many labelled historical examples are available for building the evaluation set?

items.question: A parcel carrier routes about 9 million inbound customer messages a year into six categories, against a 200ms routing budget. Discovery finds a labelled corpus of 400,000 historical messages, accumulated from agents correcting the current keyword router's mistakes, and that the six categories have been unchanged for four years. The operations director asks for Claude to perform the classification. What should discovery recommend?

options.A: Use the model for all nine million messages a year, since it handles nuanced and multi-intent enquiries better than a trained classifier would.
options.B: Use the model but classify overnight in large batches, so the unit cost falls sharply without changing the approach.
options.C: Train a small supervised classifier on the labelled corpus for the routine path, reserving the model for low-confidence cases and category drift.
options.D: Decline the request, since routing is already performed by the keyword router in production and the six categories are stable.

items.question: A retail bank's head of wealth has seen a competitor's adviser assistant and instructs the architect to skip the analysis and show something working in two weeks. There is no problem statement, no baseline and no approved data access, though a small set of anonymised adviser documents is already cleared for internal experimentation. The architect has two weeks and one engineer. What is the best next step?

options.A: Decline the instruction and insist on completing problem statement, baseline and data access before any build activity begins.
options.B: Build the demo on one real adviser task with the cleared documents, capturing that task's baseline and the sponsor's reactions.
options.C: Build a demonstration on synthetic adviser data spanning as many tasks as possible, to show the breadth of what is achievable.
options.D: Deliver an annotated slide walkthrough of the intended system instead, which avoids the data-access question entirely for now.

items.question: Shadowing underwriting assistants at a specialty insurer, the architect notices every one of them opens the broker's previous three submissions before quoting. No procedure mentions this, and none of them mentioned it when asked to describe their process. Asked why, one says 'you get a feel for whether they are shopping it around.' How should this be handled?

options.A: Disregard it; behaviour that appears in no documented underwriting procedure cannot be recorded as a requirement in the discovery pack.
options.B: Record a requirement that the system always retrieve the broker's previous three submissions into context before it produces a quote.
options.C: Raise it with the underwriting manager as an undocumented practice that should be stopped in the interests of consistency across the team.
options.D: Treat it as evidence that an unstated input matters, and elicit what the assistants read there and what decision it changes.

items.question: In a discovery pack, what distinguishes acceptance criteria from success criteria?

options.A: Acceptance criteria are pass-or-fail tests applied before go-live; success criteria are outcomes measured once it is in use.
options.B: Acceptance criteria are technical measures owned by engineering; success criteria are financial measures owned by finance.
options.C: Acceptance criteria are drafted and proposed by the delivery team, while success criteria are proposed by the business sponsor.
options.D: Acceptance criteria apply during the pilot phase only; success criteria apply after the full production rollout has completed.

items.question: A local authority's revenues team wants an assistant to decide and issue single-person council tax discounts end to end, with no officer in the loop. Which THREE conditions must discovery establish before that commitment can responsibly be made? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: That a wrong decision can be identified and corrected within a defined window, and that it is clear who does so.
options.B: That the system outperforms the current revenues officers in every application category on a held-out set of cases.
options.C: That any duty to give reasons for the decision can be satisfied by output the system can actually produce.
options.D: That a named accountable officer owns the automated decisions and can be identified when a resident appeals.
options.E: That the assistant can be deployed on infrastructure sitting inside the authority's own data centre estate.

items.question: A department head opens a discovery session by saying 'we need a chatbot on the intranet'. What should the architect do first?

options.A: Confirm the intranet as the channel and begin inventorying the site's content for indexing and chunking.
options.B: Explain that conversational interfaces are now a dated pattern, and propose a tool-using agent approach instead of a chatbot.
options.C: Work back to the problem: which question, asked by whom, how often, answered how today, and what an error costs.
options.D: Ask the department head to produce a written requirements document ahead of the next discovery session.

items.question: Why should the formal data access request be raised in the first days of discovery rather than once the design has been agreed?

options.A: Requests are approved more readily when they are submitted before a specific design exists for reviewers to object to.
options.B: Approval runs on queues the team does not control, so it can proceed in parallel — and its outcome can invalidate the design.
options.C: The data owner must be recorded as a co-author of the requirements document for the eventual acceptance sign-off to be valid.
options.D: Access approvals lapse after a fixed period and must be re-submitted from scratch if they are obtained too early in the project.

items.question: A hospital group proposes Claude-generated plain-language discharge medication guidance, with the claimed benefit being fewer readmissions caused by medication errors. Discovery establishes that printed guidance already exists and is clinically accurate, that a recent audit found 62% of patients report not reading it, and that the proposed delivery is the same printed sheet with improved wording. What should discovery conclude about the value case?

options.A: The value case holds: clearer, plain-language wording will increase the share of patients who read the discharge sheet and act on it.
options.B: The value case fails, because readmission rates are influenced by too many clinical factors to be attributed to any single intervention.
options.C: The benefit needs a behaviour change the current channel fails to produce, so test delivery before treating wording as the constraint.
options.D: Commission a health-literacy specialist to rewrite the guidance once, since a one-off content improvement does not require a system at all.

items.question: An architect is thirty minutes into a discovery workshop at a media company on rights-clearance checking. Which TWO observations most strongly indicate that the wrong people are in the room? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Participants disagree with one another about which rights categories are hardest to clear and why.
options.B: Participants ask the architect what comparable media companies have already implemented elsewhere.
options.C: Every description of how a case is handled is prefaced with 'I think what they usually do is…'.
options.D: Participants raise obscure clearance edge cases from memory that the architect had not considered.
options.E: Asked to pull up five recently cleared items, nobody present has access to the clearance system.

items.question: A stakeholder states that the system 'must be explainable'. What must be established first to turn that into a testable requirement?

options.A: Whether the model can be configured to expose its intermediate reasoning tokens to the caller.
options.B: Whether a smaller model tier would be inherently more interpretable to reviewers than a larger one.
options.C: Whether the provider publishes interpretability research and documentation for the model in use.
options.D: Who needs the explanation, at what moment, and what action they will take on the basis of it.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's medical affairs team asks for an assistant to answer questions about internal study protocols. In week two the architect discovers that another division built a Claude-based protocol question-answering system eight months ago; it is in production with about forty users, and its corpus covers roughly 70% of the documents medical affairs named. The remaining 30% sits in a different repository. The two teams have never spoken. What is the best next step?

options.A: Bring the two teams together, run medical affairs' real questions against the existing system, and scope the gap as the delivery.
options.B: Proceed with a separate build, since the existing system was designed around a different division's questions, needs and corpus.
options.C: Recommend that medical affairs adopt the existing system as it stands, with no corpus extension, and close the request.
options.D: Escalate the duplication to the group AI governance board and pause both efforts pending a formal consolidation review by architecture.

items.question: A travel company's business case for a Claude rebooking assistant assumes 120,000 disruption contacts a year, taken from the contact centre's 'disruption' call-reason code. Discovery samples 300 of those calls: 44% are general itinerary questions miscoded by agents at wrap-up, and a further 9% are genuine disruptions on bookings made through a third party the company cannot rebook. What should the architect do with the value case?

options.A: Proceed as planned; the 44% miscoding rate will fall once contact-centre agents are retrained on call-reason coding as part of the rollout.
options.B: Proceed, but apply a flat 20% reduction to the projected benefit as a general prudence adjustment to the business case.
options.C: Re-derive addressable volume from the sample — about 47%, roughly 56,000 contacts — and restate the business case on that figure.
options.D: Discard the value case; systematically miscoded contact-reason codes make any volume estimate for this population unusable.

items.question: Discovery records every item cut from scope together with the reason for the cut and the condition under which it would be reconsidered. Which TWO purposes does that log serve? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: It discharges the internal audit requirement for documented change control over the delivery baseline agreed at the gate.
options.B: It stops the same cut item being re-argued at every steering meeting, because the recorded condition decides its return.
options.C: It supplies the evaluation set for the descoped functionality at the point that functionality is eventually built.
options.D: It allows the delivery team to price each descoped item as a chargeable change request later in the engagement.
options.E: It preserves why a cut was made, so a later team does not reinstate scope whose original blocker is still in place.

items.question: A regional health insurer can fund one of two qualified use cases. The first summarises provider contract terms for the network team: moderate measurable benefit, no member-facing output, no health data, an existing review workflow and a named owner. The second drafts member responses explaining claim denials: larger benefit, but member-facing, involving health data, subject to a regulator's requirements on how adverse decisions are explained, and the compliance function has not yet been engaged. The insurer has no Claude system in production, and its board has asked for evidence of controlled adoption before approving further investment. Which should be funded, and why?

options.A: The denial-response case, because the larger benefit justifies the additional controls and produces a far stronger narrative for the board at the next investment review.
options.B: The contract-summary case: the first build should establish the operating model on a low-exposure case while the denial case's compliance path runs in parallel.
options.C: The denial-response case, descoped so the assistant drafts only the factual sections of the letter while a person writes the explanation of the decision.
options.D: Fund both at half the requested budget, so the organisation gains delivery experience across two different risk profiles at once, within the same board window.

items.question: For a Claude-based service sold to an internal business unit, which term can reasonably be written as a contractual SLA — objectively measurable from telemetry, without adjudication — rather than an internal SLO or a best-effort aspiration?

options.A: Response latency below a stated percentile threshold, measured over a monthly window.
options.B: Factual correctness of every generated summary judged against the source documents it cites.
options.C: Byte-identical responses whenever an identical request is replayed through the same endpoint.
options.D: A stated maximum rate of unsafe outputs, applied and enforced on each individual request.

items.question: A health insurer's claims operations director will sign off on a Claude-based prior-authorisation triage assistant only if the contract states 100% accuracy on clinical-criteria matching. The system auto-approves cases meeting explicit criteria and routes roughly 30% to a nurse reviewer. A false auto-approval releases payment for care that does not meet criteria; an unnecessary escalation costs nurse time. How should the architect respond?

options.A: Replace it with a two-sided error budget: a tight cap on false auto-approvals, a looser tolerance on over-escalation, plus the sampling method and disable trigger.
options.B: Accept the 100% figure in the contract, on the basis that the nurse reviewer's sign-off on every escalated case makes the whole end-to-end process accurate.
options.C: Set the router to escalate every case to a nurse, so no case is auto-approved and the automated decision path can be certified as making no errors.
options.D: Contract to the point accuracy observed on the 300-case pilot set, writing it into the service schedule as the guaranteed level for all future traffic.

items.question: A broadcaster's editorial tooling team runs a Claude-based headline-variant generator at temperature 0. Legal asks for a written statement that, given the same article, the system will always produce the same headline set, so a published headline can be reproduced during a regulatory complaint investigation up to two years later. What should the architect commit to instead?

options.A: Confirm the statement as written and cite temperature 0 to legal, since greedy decoding always selects the highest-probability token.
options.B: Pin the model to a fixed dated snapshot in the API call, which removes the remaining sources of variation and makes the sampling path fully deterministic.
options.C: Put a response cache in front of the call keyed on the article hash, so a repeat of the same article returns the stored variant set instead of a fresh generation.
options.D: Commit to producing an immutable stored record of the request, the returned variants and the model and prompt versions, rather than to regenerating the output.

items.question: A logistics operator is standardising architecture decision records for its Claude-based freight-exception triage service. Reviewers keep rejecting ADRs whose Consequences section lists only the benefits of the chosen option. What must that section add beyond the benefits for the record to do its job?

options.A: The eval scores and latency measurements that justified the choice, so the record is backed by evidence.
options.B: The recurring work the decision adds, the options it forecloses, and the conditions that should trigger a revisit.
options.C: A likelihood-and-impact risk rating for the decision, agreed with the operational risk function and reviewed each quarter.
options.D: The alternatives that were rejected, each recorded with the cost or capability reason it lost on.

items.question: A team reverses an architectural decision that was recorded in an ADR already marked accepted. What is the conventional way to record the reversal?

options.A: Edit the original ADR in place so its Decision section describes the decision now in force.
options.B: Write a new ADR for the new decision and mark the original superseded, leaving its text unchanged.
options.C: Delete the original ADR and renumber the sequence so the record holds only decisions in force.
options.D: Append the reversal to the original ADR's Consequences section as a dated follow-on note.

items.question: A national tax authority's programme board approved a Claude-based taxpayer-correspondence drafting service on a business case whose entire cost line was projected per-token API spend. Twelve months on, the actual annual run cost is materially higher than the case predicted. Which TWO of the following are recurring annual costs of owning this system that an API-spend-only case structurally omits? (Choose TWO.)

options.A: Human review of drafted correspondence before it is issued, staffed in proportion to volume.
options.B: Re-labelling the evaluation set as correspondence templates and tax policy change.
options.C: The integration work connecting the service to the existing case-management system.
options.D: The per-token input and output charges for the drafting call, at the contracted tier rate.
options.E: Purchase and refresh of GPU capacity to serve the model in the authority's own data centre.

items.question: A grocery retailer's shared-services lead presents a Claude-based supplier-invoice query assistant with an annual benefit of just under £317,000, derived as 40 accounts-payable clerks × 1.5 hours saved per day × 220 working days × £24 per hour fully loaded. No headcount reduction is planned and invoice volume is flat. The finance business partner asks where the £317,000 will appear in next year's budget. What is the right correction to the narrative?

options.A: Keep the £317,000 in the benefits table and attach a ±20% range to the hours-saved input, so the estimation uncertainty is visible to finance.
options.B: Recompute at a marginal rather than fully loaded hourly rate, producing a smaller figure the finance business partner is more likely to accept.
options.C: Reclassify it as released capacity, quoting as cash only what finance commits to convert: absorbed growth, retired contractor spend, or lower establishment.
options.D: Withdraw the productivity benefit and rebuild the case on invoice-error reduction and duplicate-payment recovery, which land directly in the profit and loss.

items.question: A law firm's innovation partner asks why the team is 'spending on retrieval plumbing instead of just fine-tuning Claude on our forty years of matter files'. Error analysis of 400 production queries shows the dominant failure is that answers cite superseded versions of the firm's precedent clauses; when the current clause is placed in context, the model applies it correctly. What is the strongest argument against fine-tuning here?

options.A: Fine-tuning would freeze the corpus as it stood at training time, superseded clauses included, so the failure persists and re-indexing cannot fix it.
options.B: Fine-tuning is unsuitable for open-ended generation; it applies to classification and extraction, while drafting is steered by prompting alone.
options.C: Fine-tuning is the technically correct fix here, but building a supervised set from forty years of matter files makes the labelling effort unaffordable.
options.D: Fine-tuning cannot be used where outputs must carry citations back to the underlying matter files, since weights hold no document identifiers to cite.

items.question: A telco's care-automation team runs a Claude-based billing-dispute resolver on 40% of eligible traffic. Overnight, the regression suite's refund-eligibility slice drops from 0.91 to 0.84; the cause is traced within the hour to a supplier changing the format of an upstream tariff feed. Customer complaint volumes are unchanged, but the team knows complaint data lags by several days. The steering committee meets in three hours. What is the best next step?

options.A: Report it to the committee as a live customer-impacting incident and recommend disabling the resolver entirely until the supplier restores the old feed format.
options.B: Hold reporting until the complaint dashboard confirms real-world impact, since one eval slice may not reflect the production traffic mix.
options.C: Route the refund-eligibility slice to human review now, then give the committee the measured drop, the upstream cause, and when customer impact will be visible.
options.D: Re-baseline the regression suite against the new tariff-feed format so the suite reflects current upstream reality, and report the slice as passing.

items.question: An agri-food processor's quality team ran a 45-case eval of a Claude-based non-conformance report classifier: 41 correct. On the same 45 cases the incumbent rule engine scored 40 correct. The programme lead wants the board slide to read '91.11% accuracy versus the incumbent's 88.89%'. What is the substantive problem with presenting it this way?

options.A: Two decimal places assert a resolution finer than one case is worth, and the whole gap is a single case, which this sample cannot separate from noise.
options.B: Nothing is wrong — both figures come from the same 45 cases, so the comparison is paired and the difference can be reported as real.
options.C: The incumbent's score should be dropped, because comparing a deterministic rule engine against a probabilistic model on accuracy alone is not meaningful.
options.D: Accuracy should be replaced by a model-graded rubric score on the same cases, the appropriate metric for a non-conformance classification task.

items.question: An airline's digital lead must brief the CFO on whether to fund the next tranche of a Claude-based disruption re-accommodation assistant. Engineering has supplied: 4,200 input and 600 output tokens per turn, 3.1 turns per conversation, on the mid capability tier, plus the fallback rate to a contact-centre agent. How should the cost story be framed?

options.A: Total platform spend for the last quarter charged to the digital cost centre, set against the same quarter last year, so the trend is visible.
options.B: The token volumes and turn counts alongside the contracted per-token rate, letting finance derive the totals themselves from the underlying drivers.
options.C: Cost per passenger successfully re-accommodated, inference plus the fallback conversations, against the current contact-centre cost per passenger.
options.D: A comparison of the airline's total AI spend against published estimates of what comparable full-service carriers spend on AI programmes.

items.question: In risk communication, what distinguishes a calibrated statement from one that is merely hedged?

options.A: It avoids technical vocabulary so that a non-specialist audience can act on it without translation.
options.B: It attributes the judgement to the risk function rather than asserting the speaker's own view.
options.C: It expresses the exposure in monetary terms, since that is the only unit an executive committee can compare across risks.
options.D: It carries a stated likelihood or range, the evidence the estimate rests on, and what would move it.

items.question: A grid operator is negotiating an internal SLO for a Claude-based outage-notification drafting service used by control-room staff. The request path is: retrieval from the asset database, a guardrail classifier, the model call streamed to the operator's screen, and an output validator. Product proposes 'p95 under 3 seconds'. Which THREE conditions must the SLO definition state before that target is measurable and defensible? (Choose THREE.)

options.A: Whether the three seconds runs to first token on the operator's screen or to the fully validated final draft.
options.B: The measurement window and the request population the percentile covers, including whether retries and fallbacks are counted.
options.C: What counts as a served request when the guardrail blocks the draft or the output validator rejects it.
options.D: The temperature and top-p settings used for the drafting call, since sampling parameters govern token-by-token latency variance.
options.E: A per-request cost ceiling, so the latency target cannot be met simply by moving every call to a higher capability tier.

items.question: A pharmaceutical company's data-science director circulates a public leaderboard showing a competing vendor's model ahead on a general reasoning benchmark, and asks why the team has not switched its pharmacovigilance case-narrative summariser. The team maintains an eval set of 800 adjudicated adverse-event narratives scored against a clinical rubric, plus format and latency requirements from the safety database. What should the architect propose?

options.A: Run the challenger on the existing 800-case eval and the format and latency requirements, and price the switch cost alongside any measured gain.
options.B: Explain that public reasoning leaderboards are contaminated by training-set leakage and should therefore play no part in any model-selection decision.
options.C: Move a canary slice of live narrative traffic to the challenger immediately, since the benchmark gap is sufficient evidence to justify a controlled trial.
options.D: Explain that the summariser's prompts and rubric are tuned to the incumbent, so the pipeline cannot be ported without a full rewrite.
